p: The Ge'ez says sixty lambs; the Latin says seven. Goes with the next entry.

readings.plain: sixty lambs

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: seven lambs

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Latin. Every other number in the verse is a multiple of seven (14, 28, 49), and the Latin's seven and twenty-one complete the pattern. Charles, with Rönsch, explains the Ge'ez sixty as a confusion of two Greek numeral letters. This is one of the few places where the Plain English Translation leaves VanderKam's Ge'ez.

p: The Ge'ez says twenty-nine; the Latin's "one" gives twenty-one. Goes with the entry on the lambs.

readings.plain: twenty-nine young goats

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: twenty-one young goats

why: As with the lambs, the Latin keeps the pattern of sevens (21 = 3 × 7). Charles and Rönsch explain the Ge'ez nine as a confusion of the Greek words for "nine" and "one."

a: The unclean animals he gave to his son Levi
t: Gave, or did not give, to Levi?
p: Charles added "not": in his view Jacob did not give the unclean animals to Levi.

readings.orig: ወእንስሳ ፡ ርኩሰ ፡ ወሀቦ ፡ ለሌዊ ፡ ወልዱ (wäʾnəssa rəkusä wähäbo lälewi wäldu)
readings.en: and the unclean animals he gave to Levi his son
readings.plain: The unclean animals he gave to his son Levi

readings.w: Charles's emendation (Charles 1902), a negative he supplied himself
readings.plain: The unclean animals he did not give to his son Levi

why: VanderKam's Ge'ez text has "he gave," and so did the Ge'ez Charles edited: Charles writes, "I have supplied the negative." Charles supplied the negative because the Testament of Levi 9 has Jacob tithe "everything" through Levi, and he thought the text limited this to clean animals. But the Ge'ez makes sense as it stands: unclean animals cannot be sacrificed, so they become the priest's (compare Numbers 18:15 and the note on this verse).

a: all the earth that is under heaven
p: The Latin promises all blessings under heaven, not all the earth.

readings.orig: ኵላ ፡ ምድረ ፡ ዘመትሕተ ፡ ሰማይ (kʷəla mədrä zämätḥətä sämay)
readings.en: all the earth that is under heaven
readings.plain: all the earth that is under heaven

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: all the blessings that are under heaven

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez, which fits the end of the verse ("they will gather in the whole earth and inherit it"). Charles thought the Latin "perhaps" right.

a: He read everything written in them
p: The Latin says Jacob "knew" everything on the tablets.

readings.en: and he read all that was written
readings.plain: He read everything written in them

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: He knew everything written in them

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. Charles printed "knew" with the Latin, but added that the Ge'ez "read" may be right.

a: goes up into the testimony of the feast days
p: The Latin has "among the days"; Charles's manuscripts have "for a testimony" or "in peace."

readings.en: in the testimony of the days of the feast
readings.plain: goes up into the testimony of the feast days

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: is entered among the days of the feast days
goes up in peace with the feast days

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's text, which agrees with Charles's manuscripts b and d. Charles thought the verse corrupt and preferred the Latin. The meaning is unsure either way (see the note).

a: He hid at night, and in the night he went into Bilhah's house
p: The Latin says "he went in secretly by night to Bilhah." Charles thought the Ge'ez repeats itself by mistake.

readings.orig: ወተኀብአ ፡ በሌሊት ፡ ወቦአ ፡ ቤተ ፡ ባላን ፡ ሌሊተ (wätäḫäbʾä bälelit wäboʾä betä balan lelitä)
readings.en: and he hid at night and entered the house of Bilhah at night
readings.plain: He hid at night, and in the night he went into Bilhah's house

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.orig: et introivit nocte occulte ad Ballan
readings.en: and he went in secretly by night to Bilhah
readings.plain: He went secretly in the night to Bilhah

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez. Charles judged the Latin "preferable" and the second "at night" a scribe's repetition; the meaning is the same.

a: She was ashamed because of him
p: In the Latin it is Reuben who is ashamed because of Bilhah.

readings.en: and she was ashamed because of him
readings.plain: She was ashamed because of him

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.en: he was put to shame by her
readings.plain: He was ashamed because of her

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez: Bilhah lets go and Reuben runs, and 33:6 goes on with her grief. The Latin makes Reuben's shame the reason he flees. Charles gives the Latin without deciding.

p: The Latin says they "sat" (camped) under the trees.

readings.plain: hiding under the trees

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: camping under the trees

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. Charles thought the Latin right, because no other telling of this legend has the kings hide.

a: the king of Tafu, the king of Ares, the king of Seragan, the king of Selo
p: The Ge'ez has "kings" for the first four towns; the Latin has "king" for all but one.

readings.orig: ነገሥተ ፡ ታፉ ፡ ወነገሥተ ፡ አሬስ ፡ ወነገሥተ ፡ ሴራጋን ፡ ወነገሥተ ፡ ሴሎ (nägäśtä tafu wänägäśtä ʾäres wänägäśtä seragan wänägäśtä selo)
readings.en: kings of Tafu and kings of Ares and kings of Seragan and kings of Selo
readings.plain: the kings of Tafu, the kings of Ares, the kings of Seragan, the kings of Selo

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902 (Charles gives only the number)
readings.plain: the king of Tafu, the king of Ares, the king of Seragan, the king of Selo

why: There are seven kings (34:2) and seven towns, and the Ge'ez itself has "king" for the last three. Charles: "we should read 'king' and not the plural. The Latin has the singular in all the instances but one." So the Plain English Translation follows the Latin here, leaving VanderKam's Ge'ez.

p: One of Charles's four manuscripts gives Jacob 800 men.

readings.plain: six thousand men
eight hundred men

why: VanderKam's text agrees with Charles's manuscripts a, b and d. Only c has 800.

t: Zebulun's wife: Neeman, no name, or Adni?
p: VanderKam's text marks the name as doubtful; three of Charles's manuscripts lack it; the Syriac list has Adni.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989), printed in brackets with a question mark
readings.plain: Zebulun's wife was [Neeman]
Zebulun's wife is not given

readings.w: Syriac list of the patriarchs' wives, as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: Zebulun's wife was Adni

why: The Plain English Translation gives the name VanderKam's text prints, in square brackets, because it is the weakest name in the list. Charles marks it with daggers as doubtful and thought it might be "the invention of an Ethiopic scribe," since his manuscripts a, b and d leave it out.

readings.en: and mercy will be on me
readings.plain: mercy will be on me

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: the Lord's mercy will be on me

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. The meaning is the same: the mercy is God's.

a: After this I too worshiped him
p: Charles changed the Ge'ez "and after this" to "and how."

readings.en: and after this I too worshiped him
readings.plain: After this I too worshiped him
Remember how I too worshiped him

why: The Ge'ez reads "and after this" (wäʾməz). Charles's note says he emended this word (waemze) to "and how" (wakama), so that the sons are told to remember Isaac's own worship. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez. "After this" may mean after Abraham's time or from then on; the text does not say which.

a: I am making this larger share greater
p: Charles changed the Ge'ez "I make great" to "I will give."

readings.plain: I am making this larger share greater
I will give this larger share

why: All the manuscripts have "I make great." The Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: for you have not been a brother to me
t: "You have not been" or "I will not be"?
p: One of Charles's manuscripts makes Esau say, "I will not be a brother to you."

readings.en: for you have not been a brother to me
readings.plain: for you have not been a brother to me

readings.en: I will not be a brother to you
readings.plain: for I will not be a brother to you

why: VanderKam's text agrees with Charles's manuscripts a, b and c. Charles thought the whole line out of place (see the note).

a: with us he is held in honor
t: "Held in honor" or "let us give him honor"?
p: The Latin has "let us give him (honor)." Charles followed it.

readings.plain: with us he is held in honor

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.plain: let us give him this honor

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez, which gives good sense: the sons honor their uncle and will not kill him. Charles changed one letter to agree with the Latin.

p: The Latin adds that the arrow struck Esau "on his right breast."

readings.en: and shot him, Esau his brother
readings.plain: struck his brother Esau

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902 (Charles gives only the sense)
readings.plain: struck his brother Esau on his right breast

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. Charles added the words from the Latin and the Yalkut, which also has Esau struck "on the right breast." The Ge'ez has the matching "left breast" only for Aduran in 38:3.
